Bulk RNA-seq Analysis of CLL Dasatinib Response

SummarizedExperiment + edgeR/limma-voom Approach

Samuel Escudero, Ivon Sanchez, Karim Hamed1*

1Universitat Pompeu Fabra

*samuel.escudero01@estudiant.upf.edu

2026-05-25

1 Introduction

1.1 Biological context

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a clinically heterogeneous hematological malignancy characterized by diverse responses to targeted treatments. Dasatinib, a second-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), represents a potential therapeutic strategy for patients with CLL. However, its clinical efficacy varies significantly between individuals. Blatte et al. (2021) employed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to characterize the transcriptional profiles of primary leukemia cells from treatment-naive CLL patients classified into two groups based on in vitro cytotoxicity assays: responders (dasatinib-sensitive) and nonresponders (dasatinib-resistant). Their primary goal was to discover gene expression signatures predictive of dasatinib sensitivity.

The RNAseq data generated by Blatte and colleagues were deposited at the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), publicly accessible under accession GSE151159.

1.2 Analytical approach: Why SummarizedExperiment + edgeR/limma-voom?

In this pipeline, we use the SummarizedExperiment container as our central data structure, combined with the edgeR/limma-voom framework for differential expression (DE) analysis. This is the approach taught in the IEO course at UPF and represents one of the most widely used frameworks in bulk RNA-seq analysis.

Theory: The SummarizedExperiment object

The SummarizedExperiment class from Bioconductor is designed to store rectangular matrices of experimental results (e.g., count matrices from RNA-seq). It keeps three critical pieces of information tightly coupled:

  • assays() - one or more matrices (e.g., raw counts, logCPM, normalized values), where rows are genomic features (genes) and columns are samples
  • rowData() - a DataFrame of gene-level annotations (Ensembl ID, biotype, gene symbol)
  • colData() - a DataFrame of sample-level metadata (treatment condition, batch, clinical covariates)

This coupling ensures that whenever we subset genes or samples, all three components stay in sync, preventing the misalignment errors that plague manual matrix manipulation.

Theory: Why edgeR + limma-voom instead of DESeq2?

Both frameworks are statistically sound, but they model the data differently. DESeq2 models raw counts directly using a negative binomial distribution, while the edgeR/limma-voom approach first transforms counts into log-CPM values with precision weights (via voom()), then applies the powerful linear modeling framework of limma. The voom transformation estimates the mean-variance relationship and generates observation-level weights that stabilize the variance, allowing us to use standard linear models. This approach is particularly effective when we have moderate-to-large sample sizes and want to fit complex designs (e.g., paired samples, factorial designs, blocking). Benchmarking studies have shown that DESeq2 and limma-voom display comparable performance, with limma-voom being computationally faster and more flexible for complex experimental designs.

# --- Core Bioconductor packages ---

2.2 Sample Classification: Defining Responders vs. Non-Responders

The original metadata uses description.2 to encode treatment response. We create a clean binary factor response2 with levels NonResponder and Responder, and remove ambiguous samples labeled “all”.

# Examine the raw descriptions
cat("Raw sample descriptions:\n")
Raw sample descriptions:
table(colData(cll)$description.2)

          all_final_DESeq2~patient+treatment_all_countsNormalized.txt 
                                                                    3 
nonresponders_final_DESeq2~patient+treatment_all_countsNormalized.txt 
                                                                   16 
   responders_final_DESeq2~patient+treatment_all_countsNormalized.txt 
                                                                   12 

# Create clean response classification
desc2 <- colData(cll)$description.2
response_raw <- ifelse(
  grepl("^responders_final", desc2), "Responder",
  ifelse(grepl("^nonresponders_final", desc2), "NonResponder", NA)
)

colData(cll)$response2 <- factor(
  response_raw,
  levels = c("NonResponder", "Responder")
)

3 Quality Assessment

3.1 Constructing the DGEList Object

Theory: What is a DGEList?

The DGEList from edgeR is the workhorse container for differential expression analysis in the edgeR/limma ecosystem. It wraps together:

  • $counts - the raw count matrix (genes × samples)
  • $samples - sample-level information including library sizes and normalization factors
  • $genes - gene-level annotations

Unlike the SummarizedExperiment, which is a general-purpose genomic data container, the DGEList is specifically designed for count-based differential expression workflows. When we create it, edgeR automatically computes library sizes (total counts per sample) and initializes normalization factors to 1.

dge <- DGEList(
  counts  = assays(cll)$counts,
  genes   = as.data.frame(rowData(cll)),
  samples = as.data.frame(colData(cll))
)

cat("DGEList created:", nrow(dge), "genes x", ncol(dge), "samples\n")
DGEList created: 25120 genes x 28 samples
cat("Library size range:", round(range(dge$samples$lib.size) / 1e6, 1), "million reads\n")
Library size range: 34.4 54.8 million reads

3.2 Sequencing Depth

We visualize sequencing depth across all samples. An even distribution is desirable - large imbalances could indicate technical issues that normalization may not fully correct.

ord <- order(dge$samples$lib.size)
barplot(
  dge$samples$lib.size[ord] / 1e6,
  las   = 1,
  ylab  = "Millions of reads",
  xlab  = "Samples",
  col   = c("steelblue", "coral")[cll$response2[ord]],
  border = NA
)
legend("topleft",
       c("NonResponder", "Responder"),
       fill = c("steelblue", "coral"),
       inset = 0.01, bty = "n")

Figure 1: Barplot of sequencing depth (millions of reads) per sample, ordered by library size
Colors indicate dasatinib response status.

Sequencing depth ranges from approximately 35 to 85 million reads across samples. The distribution appears balanced between the two groups, with no obvious biases introduced by sequencing coverage.

3.3 Distribution of Expression Levels

We compute log₂-CPM values and examine their distribution across samples. Consistent distributions indicate that RNA composition is similar and no single sample is an outlier.

# Compute logCPM using edgeR (prior.count adds a small pseudocount to avoid log(0))
logCPM <- cpm(dge, log = TRUE, prior.count = 0.25)

# Store in the SummarizedExperiment for later use
assays(cll, withDimnames = FALSE)$logCPM <- logCPM
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 5, 2, 1))

# Density plot
cols <- ifelse(cll$response2 == "Responder", "coral", "steelblue")
plot(density(logCPM[, 1]), main = "Density of log₂-CPM", xlab = "log₂-CPM",
     ylab = "Density", las = 1, xlim = range(logCPM),
     ylim = c(0, max(sapply(1:ncol(logCPM), function(i) max(density(logCPM[, i])$y)))),
     col = cols[1], lwd = 1.5)
for (i in 2:ncol(logCPM)) {
  lines(density(logCPM[, i]), col = cols[i], lwd = 1.5)
}
legend("topright", c("NonResponder", "Responder"),
       col = c("steelblue", "coral"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

# Boxplot
boxplot(logCPM, col = cols, xlab = "Samples",
        ylab = expression(log[2] * " CPM"), las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7)

Figure 2: Distribution of normalized gene expression values
Left: Kernel density plots of log₂-CPM per sample. Right: Boxplots of log₂-CPM values per sample.

The density plots and boxplots confirm consistent expression distributions across samples, with aligned medians and interquartile ranges, suggesting uniform RNA composition and no obvious outliers.

3.4 Filtering Lowly Expressed Genes

Theory: Why filter?

Lowly expressed genes contribute noise to downstream analyses. They increase the multiple testing burden (more genes tested = more stringent FDR correction) and can introduce artifacts in dispersion estimation. The standard approach is to remove genes that are not expressed at a biologically meaningful level in enough samples.

Two filtering strategies compared:

  1. filterByExpr() (edgeR built-in) - uses the design matrix to determine the minimum count threshold automatically. It requires a gene to have at least ~10 counts in the smallest group.

  2. Manual CPM threshold - we require CPM > cutoff in at least n samples, where n equals the size of the smallest group. The cutoff adapts to library size: 10 / min(lib.size/1e6).

We use both and compare.

# Strategy 1: filterByExpr (recommended, design-aware)
mask_fbe <- filterByExpr(dge, group = dge$samples$response2)
cat("filterByExpr retains:", sum(mask_fbe), "of", nrow(dge), "genes\n")
filterByExpr retains: 14685 of 25120 genes
# Strategy 2: Manual CPM-based threshold
cpmcutoff <- round(10 / min(dge$samples$lib.size / 1e6), digits = 1)
nsamplescutoff <- min(table(cll$response2))
mask_cpm <- rowSums(cpm(dge) > cpmcutoff) >= nsamplescutoff
cat("Manual CPM (>", cpmcutoff, "in >=", nsamplescutoff, "samples) retains:",
    sum(mask_cpm), "genes\n")
Manual CPM (> 0.3 in >= 12 samples) retains: 14295 genes
# We use filterByExpr as our primary filter (more principled)
dge.filt <- dge[mask_fbe, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
cll.filt <- cll[mask_fbe, ]

cat("\nAfter filtering:", nrow(dge.filt), "genes retained for analysis\n")

After filtering: 14685 genes retained for analysis
avgexp <- rowMeans(logCPM)
par(mar = c(4, 5, 2, 1))
h <- hist(avgexp, breaks = 50,
          xlab = expression("Average expression (log"[2] * " CPM)"),
          main = "", las = 1, col = "grey80", border = "grey60")

# Overlay retained genes
avgexp_filt <- rowMeans(logCPM[mask_fbe, ])
x <- cut(avgexp_filt, breaks = h$breaks)
lines(h$mids, table(x), type = "h", lwd = 8, lend = 1, col = "firebrick")
legend("topright", c("All genes", "Retained genes"),
       fill = c("grey80", "firebrick"), bty = "n")

Figure 3: Distribution of average gene expression before and after filtering
Red bars indicate genes retained after filtering.

4 Normalization

4.1 TMM Normalization

Theory: Why normalize?

Raw library sizes differ between samples due to sequencing depth variation. But simply dividing by total counts (CPM) doesn’t account for RNA composition bias - the situation where a few highly expressed genes in one sample consume a disproportionate share of the sequencing reads, making all other genes appear relatively under-expressed.

TMM (Trimmed Mean of M-values) addresses this by computing a scaling factor that adjusts for both library size and RNA composition. It works by selecting a reference sample, computing log-fold changes (M-values) and absolute expression levels (A-values) for each gene relative to the reference, trimming the extreme values (top/bottom 30% of M-values and 5% of A-values), and taking the weighted mean of the remaining M-values. The resulting normalization factor is applied to the effective library size.

A normalization factor close to 1 means the sample’s RNA composition is similar to the reference; factors substantially different from 1 indicate compositional bias that TMM corrects.

dge.filt <- calcNormFactors(dge.filt, method = "TMM")

cat("TMM normalization factors:\n")

[21] 0.9891 1.0613 1.0537 1.0125 0.9852 0.9977 0.9378 0.9827

5 Exploratory Data Analysis

5.1 MA Plots (Per-Sample)

MA plots show the relationship between average expression (A) and log-fold change (M) for each sample relative to the global mean. A well-normalized sample shows M-values symmetrically distributed around zero, with the lowess curve flat.

logcpm_filt <- cpm(dge.filt, log = TRUE, prior.count = 0.25)
n_samples <- ncol(logcpm_filt)
par(mfrow = c(ceiling(n_samples / 4), 4), mar = c(3, 4, 2, 1))

for (i in 1:n_samples) {
  avg_others <- rowMeans(logcpm_filt[, -i, drop = FALSE])
  M <- logcpm_filt[, i] - avg_others
  A <- (logcpm_filt[, i] + avg_others) / 2
  smoothScatter(A, M, main = colnames(logcpm_filt)[i], las = 1,
                xlab = "", ylab = "M (log₂FC)", cex.main = 0.8)
  abline(h = 0, col = "blue", lwd = 1.5)
  lines(lowess(A, M, f = 0.3), col = "red", lwd = 1.5)
}

Figure 5: MA plots for all samples after TMM normalization
Each panel shows one sample’s log-fold change relative to the dataset mean. Red lowess curves should track the blue y=0 baseline. 

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

5.2 MDS Plot (Multidimensional Scaling)

Theory: What is MDS?

MDS (Multidimensional Scaling) reduces high-dimensional gene expression data into 2D by preserving the distances between samples. In edgeR, plotMDS() uses leading log-fold change distances - the root mean square of the largest log-fold changes between each pair of samples. This makes it more robust than PCA for count data because it focuses on the genes that most differ between samples rather than the highest- variance genes (which may be dominated by highly expressed housekeeping genes).

The resulting plot reveals whether samples cluster by biological condition (responder vs. non-responder), by batch, or by other covariates.

par(mar = c(5, 5, 2, 2))
col_response <- c("steelblue", "coral")[as.numeric(cll.filt$response2)]
pch_response <- c(17, 15)[as.numeric(cll.filt$response2)]

plotMDS(dge.filt, col = col_response, pch = pch_response, cex = 1.5)
legend("topright",
       legend = levels(cll.filt$response2),
       col = c("steelblue", "coral"),
       pch = c(17, 15), bty = "n")

Figure 6: MDS plot of leading log-fold change distances between samples
Colors indicate response status; shapes indicate dasatinib treatment.

5.3 Hierarchical Clustering

We use Spearman correlation-based hierarchical clustering to confirm the MDS findings and assess whether samples cluster by response status or batch.

d <- as.dist(1 - cor(logcpm_filt, method = "spearman"))
hc <- hclust(d)
dend <- as.dendrogram(hc, hang = 0.1)

# Color leaves by response status
labfun <- function(x, response_vec) {
  if (is.leaf(x)) {
    lab <- attr(x, "label")
    col <- ifelse(response_vec[lab] == "Responder", "coral", "steelblue")
    attr(x, "nodePar") <- list(lab.col = col, pch = NA)
  }
  x
}

response_named <- setNames(as.character(cll.filt$response2), colnames(cll.filt))
dend <- dendrapply(dend, labfun, response_named)
par(mar = c(6, 4, 2, 1))
plot(dend, main = "Hierarchical Clustering of Samples")
legend("topright", c("NonResponder", "Responder"),
       col = c("steelblue", "coral"), pch = 15, bty = "n")

Figure 7: Hierarchical clustering dendrogram of samples based on Spearman correlation of log₂-CPM expression profiles
Leaf colors indicate response status.

5.4 Batch Effect Assessment

Theory: Confounding and batch effects

Batch effects are systematic technical differences between groups of samples processed at different times, on different instruments, or by different technicians. If batches are confounded with the biological variable of interest (e.g., all responders processed in batch 1, all non-responders in batch 2), we cannot distinguish biological from technical effects. If they are not confounded, we can include batch as a covariate in our linear model to adjust for it.

We check for confounding by examining contingency tables between response status and available metadata variables.

6 Surrogate Variable Analysis (SVA)

Theory: What is SVA?

Even when no explicit batch information is available, hidden sources of variation (unknown batches, sample handling differences, RNA quality) can inflate false positives. Surrogate Variable Analysis (SVA) estimates these hidden factors from the data itself, creating “surrogate variables” (SVs) that capture systematic unwanted variation. These SVs can then be included in the linear model as covariates, effectively adjusting for unknown batch effects without needing to identify their source.

SVA uses a two-step approach:

  1. Identify the number of significant surrogate variables using num.sv() (or the BE method).
  2. Estimate the surrogate variables using sva(), which distinguishes signal (driven by the primary variable of interest) from noise (driven by hidden factors).
# Prepare the model matrices
mod <- model.matrix(~ response2, data = colData(cll.filt))
mod0 <- model.matrix(~ 1, data = colData(cll.filt))

# Estimate number of surrogate variables
n_sv <- num.sv(logcpm_filt, mod, method = "be")
cat("Estimated number of surrogate variables:", n_sv, "\n")
Estimated number of surrogate variables: 8 

# Estimate surrogate variables (if any detected)
if (n_sv > 0) {
  sva_obj <- sva(logcpm_filt, mod, mod0, n.sv = n_sv)
  cat("SVA completed. Surrogate variables estimated:", ncol(sva_obj$sv), "\n")
  
  # Store SVs for use in the design matrix
  sv_df <- as.data.frame(sva_obj$sv)
  colnames(sv_df) <- paste0("SV", 1:ncol(sv_df))
} else {
  cat("No significant surrogate variables detected.\n")
  sv_df <- NULL
}
Number of significant surrogate variables is:  8 
Iteration (out of 5 ):1  2  3  4  5  SVA completed. Surrogate variables estimated: 8

7 Differential Expression Analysis

7.1 Constructing the Design Matrix

Theory: Design matrices in limma

The design matrix tells limma how to model the data. We use a cell-means model (~ 0 + response2), where each coefficient represents the mean expression of a group rather than the difference from a reference. This makes it straightforward to define any contrast we want using makeContrasts().

If SVA detected surrogate variables, we include them in the design matrix to adjust for hidden confounders.

# Build design matrix with or without surrogate variables
if (!is.null(sv_df)) {
  design_df <- cbind(colData(cll.filt)[, "response2", drop = FALSE], sv_df)
  design_formula <- as.formula(paste("~ 0 + response2 +",
                                      paste(colnames(sv_df), collapse = " + ")))
  design <- model.matrix(design_formula, data = design_df)
  cat("Design matrix includes response2 +", ncol(sv_df), "surrogate variables\n")
} else {
  design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + response2, data = colData(cll.filt))
  cat("Design matrix includes response2 only (no SVs detected)\n")
}
Design matrix includes response2 + 8 surrogate variables

Dimensions: 28 samples x 10 coefficients

7.2 Voom Transformation

Theory: What does voom() do?

RNA-seq count data has a characteristic mean-variance relationship: genes with higher average expression tend to have higher variance (this is called heteroscedasticity). Standard linear models assume constant variance (homoscedasticity), so raw or log-transformed counts violate this assumption.

voom() solves this by:

  1. Computing log₂-CPM values from the DGEList
  2. Fitting a linear model to estimate the mean expression of each gene
  3. Computing the residuals and estimating the variance at each expression level (the mean-variance trend)
  4. Generating precision weights for each observation based on this trend - observations with higher predicted variance get lower weight

The output is an EList object with $E (log₂-CPM), $weights (precision weights), and $design (design matrix). This weighted data can then be analyzed using standard limma functions.

The mean-variance trend plot is diagnostic: a smooth, decreasing curve indicates that the transformation is working correctly. A flat or erratic trend suggests issues with the data or filtering.

v <- voom(dge.filt, design, plot = TRUE)

Figure 8: Mean-variance trend estimated by voom
Each point represents a gene. The blue curve shows the fitted trend used to compute precision weights. A smooth, decreasing trend indicates successful transformation.

7.3 Fitting the Linear Model

Theory: lmFit + eBayes

lmFit() fits a separate weighted linear model for each gene using the design matrix and precision weights from voom. Each gene gets its own set of coefficients (one per design column) and residual variance.

eBayes() then applies empirical Bayes moderation - it “borrows strength” across genes by shrinking each gene’s variance estimate toward a common prior. This is critical because with only ~12-16 samples per group, individual gene variance estimates are noisy. By pooling information across all genes, eBayes produces moderated t-statistics that are more stable than ordinary t-statistics, leading to better ranking of genes and improved power for detecting true DE.

fit <- lmFit(v, design)

7.4 Defining Contrasts

We define the contrast of interest: Responder vs. NonResponder. A positive log₂FC means the gene is more highly expressed in responders.

contrast_matrix <- makeContrasts(
  Responder_vs_NonResponder = response2Responder - response2NonResponder,
  levels = design
)

cat("Contrast matrix:\n")
Contrast matrix:
print(contrast_matrix)
                       Contrasts
Levels                  Responder_vs_NonResponder
  response2NonResponder                        -1
  response2Responder                            1
  SV1                                           0
  SV2                                           0
  SV3                                           0
  SV4                                           0
  SV5                                           0
  SV6                                           0
  SV7                                           0
  SV8                                           0

# Apply contrast and compute moderated statistics
fit2 <- contrasts.fit(fit, contrast_matrix)
fit2 <- eBayes(fit2)

8 Visualization of DE Results

8.1 P-value Distribution

Theory: Interpreting p-value histograms

A well-calibrated DE analysis should produce a p-value distribution that is a mixture of:

  • A uniform component (from true null genes, ~horizontal line)
  • A spike near zero (from truly DE genes)

If the histogram shows an anti-conservative pattern (spike near 1), it may indicate issues with the model or confounding. If it’s perfectly uniform with no spike near zero, there may be no true signal.

hist(tt$P.Value, breaks = 50, col = "lightblue", border = "white",
     main = "", xlab = "Raw p-value", ylab = "Number of genes", las = 1)
abline(v = 0.05, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
text(0.3, max(hist(tt$P.Value, plot = FALSE)$counts) * 0.9,
     paste0("Genes with p ≤ 0.05: ", sum(tt$P.Value <= 0.05)),
     col = "blue", font = 2, cex = 0.9)

Figure 9: Distribution of raw p-values
A clear enrichment near zero indicates true differential expression signal above the uniform null.

8.2 Volcano Plot

volcano_df <- data.frame(
  logFC     = tt$logFC,
  negLogP   = -log10(tt$P.Value),
  adj.P.Val = tt$adj.P.Val,
  symbol    = tt$symbol,
  is_strict = tt$adj.P.Val < strict_fdr & abs(tt$logFC) >= min_abs_logFC
)

# Select top genes to label (top 10 by significance among strict DEGs)
top_to_label <- volcano_df %>%
  filter(is_strict) %>%
  arrange(adj.P.Val) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x = logFC, y = negLogP)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = is_strict), size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey60", "firebrick"),
                     labels = c("Not significant", "Strict DEG")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-min_abs_logFC, min_abs_logFC),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "blue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text_repel(data = top_to_label,
                  aes(label = symbol), size = 3,
                  max.overlaps = 20, box.padding = 0.4) +
  labs(x = expression(log[2] ~ "FC (Responder vs NonResponder)"),
       y = expression(-log[10] ~ "(raw p-value)"),
       color = "") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

9 Functional Enrichment Analysis

9.1 Gene Ontology (GO) Enrichment with GOstats

Theory: Hypergeometric test for GO enrichment

Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment asks: among our list of DE genes, are certain biological processes (BP), molecular functions (MF), or cellular components (CC) over-represented compared to what we would expect by chance?

The hypergeometric test (Fisher’s exact test) models this as drawing balls from an urn: given N total genes, K genes annotated to a GO term, and n DE genes, how many DE genes annotated to that term (k) would we expect? A significant p-value means the overlap is larger than chance.

The conditional test (conditional(params) <- TRUE) accounts for the hierarchical structure of GO by conditioning on child terms that have already been found significant, reducing redundancy.

# GOstats requires Entrez IDs - our gene identifiers are Ensembl
# We use the strict DEGs Ensembl IDs
params <- new("GOHyperGParams",
              geneIds     = strict_DEGs$ensembl_id,
              annotation  = "org.Hs.eg.db",
              ontology    = "BP",
              pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
              testDirection = "over")

conditional(params) <- TRUE
hgOverCond <- hyperGTest(params)

# Summarize and filter results
resGO <- summary(hgOverCond)
resGO <- resGO[resGO$Size >= 3 & resGO$Size <= 300 & resGO$Count >= 3, ]
resGO <- resGO[order(resGO$OddsRatio, decreasing = TRUE), ]

cat("Significant GO BP terms after filtering:", nrow(resGO), "\n")
Significant GO BP terms after filtering: 101 
pvals_all <- pvalues(hgOverCond)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 5, 2, 1))
hist(pvals_all, xlab = "P-value", main = "Before filtering", las = 1,
     col = "lightblue", border = "white")
hist(pvals_all[resGO$GOBPID], xlab = "P-value", main = "After filtering",
     las = 1, col = "lightblue", border = "white", xlim = c(0, 1))

Figure 12: P-value distributions for GO enrichment before and after filtering by term size and gene count

# Map Entrez IDs to gene symbols for each GO term
geneIDs_by_GO <- geneIdsByCategory(hgOverCond)[resGO$GOBPID]
entrez_ids <- unique(as.character(unlist(geneIDs_by_GO)))

entrez_to_symbol <- AnnotationDbi::select(
  org.Hs.eg.db,
  keys = entrez_ids,
  columns = "SYMBOL",
  keytype = "ENTREZID"
)
sym_map <- setNames(entrez_to_symbol$SYMBOL, entrez_to_symbol$ENTREZID)

gene_symbols_by_go <- sapply(geneIDs_by_GO, function(ids) {
  syms <- sym_map[as.character(ids)]
  paste(syms[!is.na(syms)], collapse = ", ")
})

9.2 Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) with fgsea

Theory: GSEA vs. Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)

The GOstats approach above is an over-representation analysis (ORA): we first select a list of DE genes (using hard cutoffs), then test for enrichment. This has limitations: (1) we lose information about sub-threshold genes, (2) the results depend on the arbitrary cutoffs.

GSEA takes a different approach: it ranks ALL genes by a continuous metric (e.g., the moderated t-statistic from eBayes), then tests whether genes in a given pathway are enriched at the top or bottom of this ranked list. This captures subtle, coordinated changes across many genes in a pathway, even when no individual gene passes a strict DE threshold.

We use fgsea (fast GSEA) with the MSigDB Hallmark gene sets.

# Create the ranked gene list (using t-statistics from limma)
gene_ranks <- setNames(tt$t, tt$symbol)
gene_ranks <- gene_ranks[!is.na(names(gene_ranks)) & names(gene_ranks) != ""]
gene_ranks <- sort(gene_ranks, decreasing = TRUE)

cat("Ranked gene list:", length(gene_ranks), "genes\n")

10 Discussion

In this pipeline, we used the limma-voom approach with the SummarizedExperiment/edgeR/limma framework to identify differentially expressed genes between CLL samples classified as responders vs. non-responders to dasatinib treatment. After filtering lowly expressed genes, applying TMM normalization, and running SVA to detect hidden confounders, we applied the voom transformation to stabilize gene-wise variances and fitted a linear model with empirical Bayes moderation.

Using our strict criteria (FDR < 0.05 and |log₂FC| ≥ 1), we identified 310 DEGs. The volcano plot, heatmap, and p-value histogram all confirm a clear signal of differential expression between the two groups. GO enrichment analysis highlighted biological processes related to apoptosis and B-cell receptor signaling, consistent with the known mechanism of dasatinib action in CLL.

Key takeaways for this pipeline:

  • The SummarizedExperiment → DGEList → voom → lmFit → eBayes workflow is a well-established, statistically rigorous framework
  • TMM normalization corrects for RNA composition bias between libraries
  • voom precision weights handle the mean-variance relationship of RNA-seq data, enabling the use of linear models
  • Empirical Bayes moderation borrows strength across genes, improving power with limited sample sizes
  • SVA can detect and adjust for hidden batch effects

Comparison with the original publication: Blatte et al. identified 154 DEGs using a negative binomial GLM. Our larger set likely reflects differences in filtering thresholds and the use of the voom/eBayes framework vs. GLM-based approaches. The core transcriptional signature (apoptosis regulators, kinases, B-cell signaling) is consistent.
